What Colombia Mayor is

Colombia Mayor is a cash transfer for older people living in poverty who have no pension. It is run by Prosperidad Social, the social department.

It was expanded at the end of 2025, lifting coverage from about 1.7 million people to roughly three million. The monthly payment rose with it.

The transfer is now about COP 230,000 a month, roughly US$74 at the official rate of 3,128.65 pesos on 18 August.

Money is paid in cycles, one for each month of the year. Beneficiaries collect through payment agents rather than at a bank branch.

For most recipients it is the only regular income they have. That is why a budget argument about it is not an accounting story.

The claim in the handover report

On Tuesday 18 August, President Abelardo De la Espriella delivered a dossier to prosecutors and the comptroller. It is called El libro de la verdad.

The document alleges 82 irregularities in the previous administration. Colombia Mayor is one of ten headline items.

It states that the programme exhausted its full-year 2026 budget in July. The five remaining cycles, from August to December, are described as unfunded.

It puts the monthly cost of those cycles at about COP 630 billion, roughly US$201 million. Sandra Suárez, the new director, announced an audit.

One point of accuracy: this is text in a report, not a statement made at a podium. Semana, which published the extract, attributes it to the document.

What the outgoing government said

Prosperidad Social rejected the accusation on 3 August, before the dossier appeared. The statement was issued under its then director, Mauricio Rodríguez Amaya.

It said the programme provides for twelve transfer cycles in 2026, and that six had been executed. Resources for continuity were guaranteed.

It also said the transfers are monthly and cannot be suspended, because suspending them would breach the programme’s own rules.

President De la Espriella had put the shortfall at COP 3.2 trillion, about US$1 billion. He said it in a broadcast on 2 August, before taking office.

He paired the figure with a promise. He told beneficiaries directly that the payments would be made.

The detail neither side is quoting

Cycles six and seven were originally scheduled to be paid together at the end of July. That double payment did not happen.

Prosperidad Social confirmed on 30 July that only one cycle would be disbursed. It said the next payment would follow once budget availability was defined.

That sentence came from the outgoing government’s own department, four days before it publicly denied any shortfall.

It is the strongest single fact in the file, and it belongs to neither camp. A department confident of its funding does not write that sentence.

The payment calendar published at the end of July carried the same caveat. It was described as subject to change according to financial availability.

Where the money was supposed to come from

The programme is costed at COP 8.4 trillion for 2026, about US$2.7 billion. The structure was set out in a national planning document from 2025.

Of that, COP 3.2 trillion was to come from the national budget and COP 1.7 trillion from a pension solidarity fund.

The remaining COP 3.5 trillion was to be co-financed by the labour ministry. That is the piece the incoming government says never materialised.

Read that against the denial and both sides can be telling the truth. Six cycles were paid, the seventh was covered, and the rest rested on the co-financing.

What has actually been paid

The sixth cycle ran from 29 July to 19 August and reached about three million people. Prosperidad Social put the outlay at COP 686 billion, near US$219 million.

No report anywhere describes that cycle being interrupted, suspended or short-paid. The collection window closed on Wednesday.

The seventh cycle is pencilled in to begin around 31 August. It has not been confirmed since the new director took office on 10 August.

Prosperidad Social has published nothing on Colombia Mayor since 3 August. The finance ministry has said nothing at all.

Why this matters beyond Colombia

A new government auditing its predecessor’s books is normal. Doing it while the earthquake bill runs to about US$9.6 billion is not.

Colombia’s fiscal room was already tight before 10 August. Every programme now competes with reconstruction for the same pesos.

For anyone holding Colombian assets, the question is not whether three million transfers get made. It is what gets cut so that they do.

The answer will come in the 2027 budget debate rather than in a dossier. Until then, treat both sets of figures as claims in an argument.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Colombia Mayor? A monthly cash transfer for older people in poverty who have no pension. It reaches about three million people and is run by Prosperidad Social. How much does Colombia Mayor pay? About COP 230,000 a month, roughly US$74 at the official rate of 3,128.65 pesos to the dollar on 18 August 2026. Has the money actually run out? Not for the cycle just paid. The sixth cycle reached about three million people and its collection window closed on 19 August. Who says the programme is unfunded? A handover report delivered to prosecutors on 18 August 2026. Prosperidad Social had denied any shortfall on 3 August, under the previous director.

World.title: Costa Rica Audit Finds 157 Unfinished Works and Safety Risks on Route 32
World.content:
A new technical audit of the Route 32 expansion has identified 157 unfinished works, unstable slopes and road-safety problems along the highway connecting central Costa Rica with Limón and the Caribbean coast. The National Laboratory of Materials and Structural Models at the University of Costa Rica (LanammeUCR), examined the expansion between the Route 4 intersection near Sarapiquí and Limón. The audit covered work carried out between April 2025 and May 2026.

Inspectors reviewed 402 items recorded as pending in partial acceptance documents for 23 sections of the project. Of those, 145 had been completed, 48 were being addressed and 157 remained open without corrective action. Inspectors could not locate or verify another 52 items.

Drainage represented the largest area of concern. The audit identified 154 drainage-related items, including 62 that remained unresolved. LanammeUCR described the situation as particularly important because the highway passes through one of Costa Rica’s rainiest regions, where poorly functioning drains can contribute to flooding, erosion and damage to the road.

Other pending work involved vehicle barriers, the road surface, pedestrian infrastructure and signs. Among the pedestrian projects reviewed, 27 of 39 remained unresolved. Inspectors also found 20 outstanding road-surface items, 16 involving vehicle containment systems such as barriers, and 16 related to signs.

The audit raised separate concerns about slope stability, particularly between kilometers 100 and 112. Inspectors documented erosion, falling material and problems controlling surface water. Two slopes, located near kilometers 101.6 and 111.5, were singled out because inspectors found no evidence that permanent solutions were being implemented. Other unstable locations were also observed along the expanded section.

The findings carry particular cause for concern during periods of heavy rainfall. Route 32 often experiences closures because of landslides and falling material, disrupting travel between San José and the Caribbean and affecting access to Limón’s ports and popular destinations such as Cahuita and Puerto Viejo.

LanammeUCR also questioned the use of roundabouts built at several intersections along the expanded highway. The roundabouts have provided temporary improvements to traffic movement, but the audit concluded that they do not replace the grade-separated intersections originally planned for a highway carrying fast-moving traffic and large numbers of heavy trucks.

Inspectors recommended monitoring the roundabouts while moving ahead with permanent solutions. Quality control was another area of concern. During some site visits, work was taking place without the presence of supervisory personnel or laboratories responsible for testing and verifying construction quality.

Tests also found trends of noncompliance in some asphalt-mixture measurements, including the size distribution of the material and the amount of space within the mixture. However, much of the cement-stabilized base material tested within the limits established in the project contract.

The audit was based on 29 technical inspection visits, 27 rounds of material sampling and a review of project records. Findings were communicated to the project administration through 16 separate notices while the audit was underway. LanammeUCR recommended completing the outstanding work, adopting permanent solutions for unstable slopes and intersections, strengthening technical supervision and improving quality controls.

The laboratory warned that unresolved drainage, barriers and pedestrian infrastructure could affect the safety, operation and long-term condition of a highway used daily by thousands of drivers.

World.title: Costa Rica Closes Turrialba Volcano and Guayabo Monument Due to Heavy Rains
World.content:
Two popular to visit in the Turrialba area have closed temporarily as continued rainfall and saturated ground raise the risk of landslides and other emergencies. The public areas of Turrialba Volcano National Park and Guayabo National Monument closed today and will remain off-limits until further notice. The measure goes for tourists, guides and government personnel working at both sites.

The National System of Conservation Areas said the closure responds to unstable weather conditions and the orange alert in effect for the canton of Turrialba. Officials will reassess both sites once the emergency period ends before deciding whether visitors can safely return. The decision is tied to the weather rather than a change in volcanic activity at Turrialba Volcano.

Authorities said the purpose is to prevent people from entering areas where heavy rain may have weakened the ground, affected trails or increased the possibility of falling material. Visitors should not attempt to enter either protected area while the closure remains in place. Tour operators and travelers with planned visits are being advised to check official updates before traveling to the area.

Guayabo National Monument protects Costa Rica’s most important pre-Columbian archaeological site. Its stone roads, aqueducts, foundations and ceremonial structures offer a look at a settlement that flourished centuries before the arrival of Europeans. Turrialba Volcano National Park, meanwhile, gives visitors access to one of the best-known active volcanoes here in Costa Rica.

The park’s location and elevation also make it particularly exposed to rapidly changing weather, strong winds and difficult trail conditions. The closures come as Costa Rica continues dealing with the effects of consecutive tropical waves. More than 1,300 people remained in emergency shelters Tuesday, while authorities delivered assistance to isolated communities in the Caribbean and mountainous Indigenous territories.

Heavy rainfall has also caused flooding, landslides and repeated road closures. Although conditions improved in some locations Tuesday, emergency officials warned that saturated soil could continue producing incidents even when rainfall temporarily decreases. SINAC will determine when Turrialba Volcano National Park and Guayabo National Monument can reopen after reviewing conditions and receiving updated guidance from emergency officials. No reopening date had been announced as of yet.

World.title: Guanacaste Airport Outpaces Costa Rica’s Main Airport
World.content:
Costa Rica welcomed more than 2 million international tourists during the first seven months of 2026, but the clearest sign of change was not simply how many people arrived. It was where they chose to land. Guanacaste Airport in Liberia recorded the strongest airport growth, reinforcing its role as the main gateway to Costa Rica’s northern Pacific beaches.

For those heading to Tamarindo, Playas del Coco, the Papagayo Peninsula or other parts of the Nicoya Peninsula, flying into Liberia can eliminate the need to cross the Central Valley and then make the long drive west. The airport’s expanding network of direct flights is making that option available to more visitors.

A total of 698,079 international tourists entered Costa Rica through the Guanacaste airport between January and July, an increase of 13.3% from the same period in 2025. In July alone, the airport received 89,947 visitors, up 12.6%. Juan Santamaría International Airport remained Costa Rica’s busiest entry point, welcoming 1,154,732 international tourists during the seven-month period. Arrivals at the Alajuela airport grew by 3.6%, including 158,076 visitors in July.

Together, the two airports accounted for most of the 2,001,660 international tourists who visited Costa Rica from January through July. The overall number was 6.4% higher than during the same period last year. Air travel continued to power the tourism industry, accounting for 1,853,430 arrivals and growing by 7%. Another 142,780 visitors entered by land or water, although arrivals through those routes declined by 1.7%.

The figures also reveal a gradual shift in where Costa Rica’s visitors are coming from. The United States remained the largest tourism market by a wide margin, sending 1,142,234 visitors during the first seven months of the year. Americans accounted for 57% of all international arrivals, but growth from the United States was almost flat at 0.4%.

That makes the performance of other international markets increasingly important. Canada recorded one of the strongest increases, with 220,691 Canadian tourists arriving between January and July, up 24.4%. Costa Rica also received 315,340 visitors from Europe, an increase of 8.4%.

Arrivals grew from North America, South America, Europe, the Asia-Pacific region, the Caribbean and the Middle East. Visitor numbers from Central America and Africa declined. The July results also brought some relief after tourism arrivals slipped in June. For hotels, vacation rentals, restaurants, transportation providers and tour companies, continued growth heading into the year-end high season would be welcome.

Still, the gains are not evenly distributed. Costa Rica’s tourism growth is increasingly being driven by Guanacaste Airport and markets such as Canada and Europe, while the much larger U.S. market remains largely unchanged. More than the two-million-visitor milestone, that changing pattern may be the most important tourism story of 2026.

World.title: What happened to Galeria Namu?
World.content:
Founded in 1998, Galeria Namu had become a must-visit attraction for tourists visiting San Jose, as well as for many nationals, interested in seeing the gallery’s curated collection of authentic ethnographic and cultural arts of Costa Rica and then, on the 30th of December, 2024, Namu was suddenly forced to shutter the gallery indefinitely.

This article is for folks who, since December 2024 – right at the beginning of Costa Rica’s annual high tourist season – would have walked up, expectingly, to Galeria Namu’s entrance on the edge of Barrio Amon, right across from the Alianza Francesa (the French Alliance) on Avenida 7, just to be met with the sad sight of the permanently shuttered locale. The large billboard still up on the wall, with its distinctive Pre-Columbian-inspired logo, would have given pedestrians the sense that the gallery was still open for business.

With the change of the building’s ownership in 2024, the gallery, that September of the same year, was given notice that the new owners were not going to renew the lease in the new year as they had “other ideas” for the space (read: we want to increase rent for another business!).

With this unexpected closure of the gallery, so ended nearly three decades of a cultural “institution” that strove, under a fair-trade business practice, to offer to a discerning public, a marvelous catalogue of Costa Rica’s national cultural arts and authentic ethnographic material culture (a subject matter, that frankly, for a highly visited Central American nation, is somewhat undocumented even today).

The good news is that Galeria Namu still exists, albeit, for now, in a digital format, with the official website having been launched in March of this present year. Namu is still receiving new pieces all the time in the three arts categories that the gallery collection has always showcased:

1. Ethnographic material culture and artistic expression created by artisans from among the 8 indigenous groups of Costa Rica

2. Faithfully rendered, museum-quality reproductions of Pre-Columbian era objects, such as those seen in the exhibition halls of the national museums, featuring goldwork, authentic jade pieces, pottery and carved stone sculpture

3. Selected Costa Rican folk arts and artes populares created by artists from different milieu, such as Afro-Caribbean traditions, artisans from campesina communties, women’s art collectives, Criollo traditions, etc. – plus other individual folk artists that “fit the bill” who wonderfully depict, through their compositions, la tiquicia and the peculiarities of Costa Rican lifeways and ambience.

Aside from the primary focus on the cultures and lifeways of Costa Rica, Galeria Namu has always given a space for some examples of indigenous cultural expression from our neighbouring naciones hermanas of Panama (ie. the Wounaan tribe), Nicaragua (ie. the Miskitu people) and Honduras (ie. the indigenous Lenca).

Just as Galeria Namu has always done over the last three decades, purchased artwork can be securely packaged for international shipping and for clients who either reside in Costa Rica, or for visitors at their accommodations, the gallery is happy to get one’s purchases to one’s residence, or hotel, free of charge – or even rendez-vous in person to hand deliver purchased artwork to clients within the GAM.

https://www.galerianamu.com/

World.title: 19-year-old pleads guilty to unlicensed Glock so sister can go free; third sibling remains at large
World.content:
19-year-old pleads guilty to unlicensed Glock so sister can go free; third sibling remains at large

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City man has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after pleading guilty to keeping a firearm without a gun licence, while the charge against his older sister was withdrawn.

Aaron Ayren Pitter, 19, and his sister, 20-year-old Gregoria Veronica Pitter, were escorted to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, where they were jointly charged in connection with a Glock 17 Gen 4 9mm pistol found during a police search of a Pitter Street residence.

Aaron initially pleaded guilty while Gregoria pleaded not guilty. The Magistrate, however, declined to immediately accept Aaron’s plea and encouraged him to seek legal advice before making the decision.

The siblings were initially remanded, but minutes later Aaron requested to be brought back before the court and again indicated that he wanted to plead guilty and accept responsibility for the firearm.

His guilty plea was accepted, and he was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until September 30, 2026, when he is expected to be sentenced following mitigation.

Following Aaron’s guilty plea, the prosecution withdrew the firearm charge against Gregoria and she was released.

Police say a third sibling, Roy Pitter Jr., remains at large.

According to police, officers from the Violence Protection and Enforcement Team executed a search warrant at a residence on Pitter Street on Monday, August 17.

During a search of the bathroom, police allegedly found a pair of blue short pants stuffed inside a hole beside the bathtub. Wrapped inside the clothing was a Glock 17 Gen 4 pistol with a magazine attached.

Police say Aaron arrived at the residence while the search was underway and, after being shown the firearm, allegedly told officers that it belonged to him and that he knew it was there.

The firearm and magazine were examined and found to contain no ammunition.

Aaron and Gregoria were subsequently detained and charged with keeping a firearm without a gun license.

World.title: Belize City fisherman remanded after allegedly sneaking into ex’s house through bedroom window and slapping her after breakup
World.content:
Belize City fisherman remanded after allegedly sneaking into ex’s house through bedroom window and slapping her after breakup

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 32-year-old Belize City fisherman has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being charged in connection with an alleged domestic dispute involving the mother of his children.

Ramzee Roman Palma, also known as “Terral Palma,” appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with burglary with intent to cause bodily harm and harm upon a 30-year-old woman.

The harm charge stems from an alleged incident on Friday, August 14, while the burglary charge relates to an incident the following day.

Palma pleaded not guilty and maintained in court that he had not entered the woman’s home. The Magistrate cautioned him against saying more about the allegations while unrepresented, explaining that he could potentially incriminate himself.

The prosecution objected to bail, citing the serious nature of the burglary allegation and concerns surrounding domestic violence cases.

Palma pleaded with the court for bail, telling the Magistrate that he has three children at home and that his imprisonment would negatively affect his family. The Magistrate, however, upheld the prosecution’s objection and remanded him to prison until October 13, 2026. He was informed of his right to apply to the High Court for bail.

According to police, the Gender Violence Response and Investigation Unit responded to a report on New Road early on August 14 and spoke with the woman, who reported that she and Palma had recently separated after being in a relationship for approximately eight years.

The woman alleged that at about 3:00 a.m. she was awakened by the sound of her bedroom window being opened and saw Palma entering the room without her permission.

She told police that an argument subsequently developed and Palma allegedly slapped her to the right side of her face, causing pain and swelling.

Police say officers observed swelling to the woman’s face and issued her medico-legal forms. A statement was recorded, and Palma was subsequently detained and charged with burglary and harm.

World.title: Former Treasury cashier fined $1,500 for stealing $5,000 from Government; Says she did it for ‘medical reasons’
World.content:
Former Treasury cashier fined $1,500 for stealing $5,000 from Government; Says she did it for ‘medical reasons’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A former Government of Belize Treasury Department cashier has been fined after changing her plea to guilty in connection with the theft of $5,000 in government funds in 2024.

Shamira Hope, 35, of South Street, Belize City, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, where she pleaded guilty to theft.

Hope had initially pleaded not guilty after being charged in 2024 but changed her plea when the matter returned to court.

As a first-time offender for theft, Hope was spared a custodial sentence. The Magistrate fined her $1,500, along with $5 in court costs. She has until November 27, 2026, to pay the $1,505 total or, in default, serve three months in prison.

The case dates back to October 2024, when officials at the Treasury Department discovered that $5,000 was missing from Hope’s cash pan.

According to the case facts, a finance officer conducted a cash check on October 2, 2024, and discovered that 100 fifty-dollar notes, totaling $5,000, were missing.

The officer reportedly confronted Hope about the missing money, and Hope allegedly admitted that she had taken the funds for medical reasons.

An assistant accountant general subsequently reported the matter to police.

Hope was later detained and taken to the Raccoon Street Police Station. Police say she declined to participate in an interview and was subsequently charged with theft.

World.title: Baghdad Street farmer gets 3 months in jail for crack pipe and unpaid fines; Tells court he does drugs because he is in consistent pain but agrees to rehab
World.content:
Baghdad Street farmer gets 3 months in jail for crack pipe and unpaid fines; Tells court he does drugs because he is in consistent pain but agrees to rehab

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 59-year-old Belize City farmer has been sentenced to prison after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe and admitting in court that he has a drug addiction.

Norman Anthony Bernard, a resident of Baghdad Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he pleaded guilty to possession of utensils used for smoking a controlled drug after police reportedly found him with a metal crack pipe on Friday, August 14.

During mitigation, the Magistrate questioned Bernard about his history of drug-related convictions and asked whether he needed help with a drug problem.

Bernard admitted that he struggles with drug addiction, telling the court that he uses drugs because he suffers from persistent pain.

“I sick, so when I smoke drugs, it ease the pain. I smoke because I have pain all deh time,” Bernard told the court.

The Magistrate sentenced him to two months’ imprisonment and asked whether he was willing to participate in a drug rehabilitation program while incarcerated. Bernard agreed to enter the program.

The court also noted that Bernard had an outstanding $305 fine from a previous conviction, toward which he had made no payments. A warrant was sent to the Belize Central Prison requiring him to serve three months in default of that unpaid fine.

That three-month term will run concurrently with the new two-month sentence, meaning Bernard is expected to serve a total of three months in prison.

World.title: “Markhelm Lizarraga must go”: UDP doubles down after union support
World.content:
“Markhelm Lizarraga must go”: UDP doubles down after union support

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The United Democratic Party says it welcomes Belize’s trade unions joining its call for the immediate removal of Markhelm Lizarraga as Chairman of Belize Telemedia Limited.

In a statement released today, the party said it was the first to demand Lizarraga’s removal after the BTL Board approved the proposed $80 million SMART/SpeedNet acquisition.

“Our position remains clear: public assets require public accountability,” the release states.

The UDP argues that Cabinet’s later rejection of the deal does not settle the matter. According to the party, the rejection “does not erase the Board’s decision or absolve its Chairman or the appointing Government of responsibility.”

The party is again calling for Lizarraga’s immediate removal, framing the issue as one of governance rather than politics.

“This is a matter of governance. Markhelm Lizarraga must go,” the statement concludes.

The proposed acquisition drew sustained public criticism before Cabinet turned it down. BTL is majority owned by the Government of Belize, and the party maintains that decisions taken at the board level on that scale demand a public accounting.

The UDP has not indicated what further steps it will take if the call is not met.

World.title: Cayo CET opens registration for Advanced Bartending Level 3
World.content:
Cayo CET opens registration for Advanced Bartending Level 3

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Cayo Centre for Employment Training is now accepting registrations for its Advanced Bartending Level 3 course, starting September 28, 2026.

The course runs Monday to Friday at the Cayo CET campus in two shifts, 8am to 12pm or 4pm to 8pm. It covers 100 contact hours over four weeks and is delivered by qualified and experienced instructors.



Applicants need at least two years of bartending experience, or a Tourism Hospitality Management Level 2 certificate.

The full course costs $800 and includes theory and practical sessions, educational trips, a bartending competition, and all materials. Participants who complete the programme receive a Cayo CET Level 3 certificate.

Bartending professionals will taste, evaluate, and grade the cocktails and beverages prepared by participants during the course.

Registration is open now. Interested persons can call 611-2944 or 824-2944, or email [email protected].

World.title: Police stopped him for riding upstop then found 0.2 grams of crack on him; $200 fine
World.content:
Police stopped him for riding upstop then found 0.2 grams of crack on him; $200 fine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 51-year-old Belize City man has been fined $205 after pleading guilty to possession of 0.2 grams of crack cocaine.

Elroy Mark Bonnell, a labourer of Castle Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with possession of a controlled drug.

Bonnell pleaded guilty and told the court in mitigation that he did not intend to waste the court’s time.

“I got caught with the drugs. I plea guilty. Am asking for a fine,” he told the court.

The Magistrate fined Bonnell $200, along with $5 in court costs. He was given until September 30, 2026, to pay, or in default, serve one month in prison.

The charge stems from an incident on Sunday, August 16, 2026.

Police say officers were conducting motorcycle patrol on Cleghorn Street when they noticed Bonnell riding contrary to traffic with a grey shirt wrapped around his head.

Officers stopped him and informed him that a search would be conducted. Police allege that when an officer removed the shirt from Bonnell’s head, a small cream-colored substance suspected to be crack cocaine fell from the shirt to the ground near his feet.

The substance was later weighed at 0.2 grams.

World.title: ‘Ah get bust’: ‘Dads’ fined $805 for 1 gram of crack but says he can afford it
World.content:
‘Ah get bust’: ‘Dads’ fined $805 for 1 gram of crack but says he can afford it

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 61-year-old Belize City man has been fined $805 after pleading guilty to possession of one gram of crack cocaine.

Louis Alfonso Romero, a labourer of Plues Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with possession of a controlled drug.

Police say Romero was found in possession of one gram of crack cocaine on Sunday, August 16, 2026.

Romero wasted no time in pleading guilty to the charge.

In mitigation, he told the court that he was working and could pay a fine, adding, “Ah get bust, ah get bust.”

Romero, who is not a first-time offender, was handed a non-custodial sentence and fined $800, along with $5 in court costs.

He has until December 30, 2026, to pay the total $805. In default of payment, he faces three months’ imprisonment.

World.title: CXC success
World.content:
Sixteen months after announcing a pilot for its Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate (CTEC) in mathematics to tackle “the perennial under-performance of students” in the subject, the Caribbean Examinations Council (CXC) on Tuesday reported an 88 per cent pass rate among the 2,535 candidates who sat the exam in the May-June 2026 sitting. A total of 2,230 candidates passed.

Dr Wayne Wesley, CXC registrar and chief executive officer, made the disclosure during the live results ceremony from Anguilla, saying the results were proof that the region has “overwhelmingly accepted CTEC”.

“I am pleased indeed, and I am proud to announce that of these 2,535 candidates who wrote CTEC module one in the mathematics pilot examinations, 88 per cent achieved acceptable grades, and across the entire Caribbean only one candidate received the lowest grade. It simply means that most candidates are benefiting from the approach. Measured against a generation in which barely one in three candidates succeed in a typical sitting, this achievement represents a remarkable turnaround,” Wesley said.

Acknowledging, however, that “a module is not a whole subject”, the CXC registrar pointed out that “the full qualification still requires completion of every module at the full standard”.

“But that is precisely what these results demonstrate. When learning is assessed in focused, achievable stages, our students do more than cope; they excel, they engage, persist, and succeed. The May-June mathematics pilot proves that the modular approach works for students, for classrooms, and for the region. This landmark result belongs to the young people who earned it,” Wesley stated.

CTEC, the new qualification which was unveiled by CXC in April 2025, is at the same standard of Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) and Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) and utilises the same syllabus.

“For years in mathematics — the subject that is foundational to every vocation in life — only about a third of our candidates have achieved acceptable grades in a typical sitting. Behind that statistic are hundreds of thousands of young people who sat in our classrooms for five years and walked away with nothing in hand to show for what they did learn. Not because they learn nothing, but because our instrument of assessment was an all-or-nothing event. One subject, one sitting, one verdict. If the verdict went against you, the system did not recognise you and stayed silent about your progress,” Wesley noted in explaining the motivation behind CTEC.

“I described CTEC as a game-changer, and I promised then that we are witnessing the beginning of the end of the Caribbean Examinations Council as we know it. Today we keep that promise and we make history in Anguilla by announcing that the achievement of the highly successful CTEC pilot in mathematics in the May/June 2026 examinations and, with the approval of our board of governors, CXC is pleased to officially launch the Caribbean Targeted Education Certificate,” the CEO said.

“At CXC we hold to the position that competence is competence, no matter how long it takes to achieve and no matter how the route and… no matter the route by which it comes. This is how things and times have changed. This is how we have to meet this generation of learners where they are,” he added.

Wesley contended that “an assessment model built in the [20th] century cannot be expected to adequately serve a 21st century generation”, but said “CTEC is assessment redesigned for learners without lowering by a single degree the standard to which we hold”.

“When we were designing CTEC we asked ourselves, would the region embrace it? Today we have proof of concept from a region that has overwhelmingly accepted CTEC. When we invited the region to pilot CTEC mathematics module 1, more than 2,500 candidates stepped forward as pioneers across 15 territories, and 42 centres from Jamaica to Belize, from Barbados to the Cayman Islands and Anguilla, which was among the first countries to sign on to the pilot. Principals told us that their students were excited about the pilot examinations,” he said.

Wesley said the modularised examination format will now be applied to four other subject areas going forward, given the success of the maths module pilot.

“This is a new day for our Caribbean learners on the strength of this CTEC mathematics pilot. The Caribbean Examinations Council is declaring to our students this simple truth: What you know counts. We hear you. We see you. Your learning has been seen, measured, and certified. You are not at the end of the road. You are on your way up the staircase,” he said.

Telling policymakers across the region that “CTEC is yours to embed in your national education strategies, in your workforce and TVET planning and second chance programmes”, Wesley said CXC’s team was ready to work with the various ministries of education across the region and will be visiting territories in the weeks ahead to do exactly that.

CXC also said the 2,535 candidates who were involved in the pilot will continue to enjoy doing the other modules free of cost.

The candidates have a four-year period to complete it and will receive CSEC certification at the end.

World.title: Saving Moo Moo
World.content:
Nicholas Thomas, a resident of Spanish Town, feeds the cow he affectionately calls Moo Moo. (Photo: Napthali Junior)

Driving along Walks Road in Spanish Town, in the vicinity of Crescent Primary School, motorists may have noticed a cow lying motionless on the side of the road in the blazing sun, in the same spot for days. That cow is affectionately called Moo Moo by community members who have been taking care of her since she was injured in an accident more than a week ago.

When the Jamaica Observer visited the area Monday, police officers were seen feeding the injured cow grass and offering her water as community members looked on. Moo Moo ate slowly, pausing between bites as she gulped down water from a Dutch pot, seemingly desperate to rehydrate after days exposed to the summer heat. She remained largely immobile with most of her legs tucked beneath her body as though to protect them from further harm.

Reports from the policemen, Constable Dwight Lewis and Leighton Taylor, are that they were passing the area on Monday when they saw the cow and stopped. Moo Moo is believed to be pregnant and was injured during a hit-and-run accident. The owner has not yet come forward, and the accident has not been reported.

In the meantime, residents have stepped in.

A registered nurse who frequents the area, Gabriel Hamilton, said she spotted the cow about a week ago and became concerned when she noticed the animal was immobile.

“I came into the community, and I was asking around. People were not sure whose animal it is. I got closer to her, and I realised that her front right leg was injured, and I saw some blood in her abdominal area as well. The members of the community also told me that she’s pregnant, and I was like, ‘No, this cannot be’,” said Hamilton, visibly distressed as she recounted the interaction.

An animal lover who almost pursed a career as a veterinarian, she said she immediately sprang into action, calling Hope Zoo, the Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA), the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) and even her friend who is a trained veterinarian. Members of the community said they also made several calls to animal-related facilities, but no one has come to help.

Determined to ensure that the animal survived, Hamilton said she and other members of the community formed a pact to take care of Moo Moo. She said she entrusted community member Nicholas Thomas to be the cow’s primary caregiver, promising to compensate him for his efforts to keep Moo Moo alive. She had noticed that Moo Moo had lost weight and she was concerned about her nutrition.

Thomas said he was happy to officially take on the role, noting that he was already providing some level of care to the animal.

“When she ready for food she say, ‘Moo, moo’ and so I call her the name Moo Moo and she just accept everything with love,” he said, laughing.

He then bent down to rub the cow’s head, later jumping with joy as he thanked the news team for stopping by to highlight the story. He said he is optimistic that Moo Moo will survive, urging anyone who can help to do so.

Constable Lewis said he has reported the incident to his supervisor, and they are working to get a member of the agriculture team on location to transport the cow and get it medical attention.

“It’s part of our duty to serve, protect, and reassure, so we are reassuring the cow that help is on the way, and we are trying to get through to see if there is any owner so the owner can come and get her. The owner might not be sure as to its whereabouts. The owner might realise that the cow is not back, but as to the actual location of the cow, the owner might not be sure, so with the help of the media, probably the owner can get in touch and then speak to the Spanish Town police,” Constable Lewis told the Observer.

Constable Taylor, who farms as a hobby, said he loves animals and had to stop to help Moo Moo.

“We just want to make sure that she stays alive until the relevant persons come. We wish we could give her some shelter, but it’s out of our hands because we can’t even lift her up, so we just a try we best to make sure she stays alive,” said Taylor.

“Everybody who is passing can give a hand because we can’t stay here the whole day with her, but each person that is passing can give an eye. I realise a lot of persons help out because we come here and see a pot with water, so that’s good. It could’ve been my animal, so it’s good to see everybody helping out,” added Taylor.

World.title: RECOVERY AHEAD OF SCHEDULE
World.content:
JAMAICA could return to pre-Hurricane Melissa levels of economic output as early as the April-to-June quarter of 2027, significantly sooner than previously expected as the year-on-year contraction in the economy narrows and reconstruction gathers momentum.

The Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ) said Tuesday that the current trajectory suggests the economy could regain the level of output recorded before Melissa within 1.5 to two years of the hurricane, compared with an earlier expectation that recovery would take about three years and extend into fiscal year 2028/29.

“Note, however, that full recovery — to include rebuilding efforts and replacing housing stock, public infrastructure and livelihoods — will be over a more extended period, possibly three to five years,” PIOJ Director General Dr Wayne Henry said at the institute’s quarterly economic briefing.

The improved outlook comes even as preliminary PIOJ estimates show that real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted 2.9 per cent in the April-to-June quarter compared with the corresponding period of 2025, marking a third-consecutive quarter of year-on-year decline.

The economy contracted 7.1 per cent year on year in the October-to-December 2025 quarter and 4.1 per cent year on year in January-March 2026.

The PIOJ, however, rejected suggestions that Jamaica is in a recession, pointing instead to the sequential improvement in economic activity following the hurricane-induced collapse in the final quarter of 2025.

“Yes, we can confirm that there is not a recession. We are not in a recession,” Senior director of the PIOJ’s Economic Planning and Research Division James Stewart told the Jamaica Observer.

Stewart said a recession also appeared unlikely for the remainder of the year.

While output in the first quarter of 2026 remained below the corresponding period a year earlier, seasonally adjusted real value added an increased 3.3 per cent compared with the hurricane-hit October-to-December quarter.

“Following three consecutive quarters of quarter-over-quarter growth during the first nine months of 2025 the economy experienced a sharp setback in the October-December 2025 quarter as Hurricane Melissa triggered a 7.3 per cent decline in real value added relative to July-September 2025,” Henry said.

“Importantly, the latest GDP release from Statin [Statistical Institute of Jamaica] confirms that the economy has begun to recover from the shock. The seasonally adjusted real value added for January-March 2026 increased by 3.3 per cent compared with the October-December 2025 quarter, signalling a rebound in economic activity,” he added.

The PIOJ, in its latest review of economic performance, said the April-to-June downturn largely reflected the lingering effects of Hurricane Melissa, which disrupted production, employment, domestic demand, and business and consumer confidence.

During the review quarter the goods-producing industry declined by an estimated 6.4 per cent as key sub-industries, including agriculture and mining and quarrying, recorded significant contractions.

Agriculture fell 17 per cent as hurricane damage across major crop-producing parishes was compounded by drought conditions associated with the El Niño phenomenon.

Mining and quarrying, on the other hand, contracted by 23.9 per cent, largely due to a 30.8 per cent decline in aluminium production as technical challenges linked to hurricane damage continued to weigh on operations.

There were, however, signs of resilience in other productive activities as manufacturing grew by an estimated one per cent while construction expanded 0.3 per cent, supported by higher civil engineering activity.

The services industry contracted by 1.7 per cent, with most industries declining. The exceptions were financial and insurance activities, up 1.9 per cent; wholesale and retail trade, repair of motor vehicles, and installation of machinery and equipment (WRTRIM), up 0.2 per cent; and public administration and defence, up 0.1 per cent.

Accommodation and food service activities, one of the larger service industries, however fell 12.2 per cent, reflecting weaker tourism activity. Preliminary data show stopover arrivals for April and May falling 19.6 per cent to 382,745 visitors, while visitor expenditure declined 17 per cent to US$578 million.

For the January to June period or first half of the calendar year real GDP is estimated to have contracted by 3.5 per cent, with the goods-producing industry down 6.8 per cent and services down 2.4 per cent.

Despite the weaker headline numbers, PIOJ Director General Dr Wayne Henry said the underlying trend points to an economy recovering from a significant one-off shock rather than entering a prolonged downturn.

Henry also pointed to developments in the labour market as another positive indicator, saying the pace of recovery reflects the resilience of Jamaica’s underlying economic fundamentals despite widespread disruption caused by the hurricane.

The PIOJ, while maintaining a negative short-term outlook, said it expects the rate of contraction to narrow as more industries recover. The institute forecasts a contraction of 0.5 per cent to 1.5 per cent in the current July-to-September quarter, followed by growth of one per cent to three per cent for fiscal year 2026/27.

“Economic growth is expected to be driven by gradual recovery in all industries, due to an expectation for fairly robust growth in the latter half of the fiscal year,” Henry said.

He said the outlook is supported by the low-base effect from Hurricane Melissa’s impact in the latter half of fiscal year 2025/26, faster recovery across most industries, increased reconstruction activity, favourable weather conditions, and the potential resolution of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

A rise in capital expenditure under the Public Sector Investment Programme is also expected to support the recovery. Spending increased 55.8 per cent to $13.7 billion during the April-to-June quarter, boosting public investment and reconstruction activity.

“This momentum is expected to continue over the short to medium term as reconstruction activities intensify and the implementation of recovery projects accelerate,” Henry said.

World.title: FUTURE KINGS!
World.content:
Jamaica’s players celebrate during the CWI Rising Stars Under-19 men’s three-day cricket final against Barbados at Arnos Vale Stadium in St Vincent on August 1, 2023. (Photo: CWI Media)

Jamaica Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says that while the Kingsmen ownership continues to find its footing with the Jamaican franchise in the Caribbean Premier League (CPL), his eyes remain fixed on the developmental aspect of their partnership.

For two years Jamaica was without a franchise in the region’s premier Twenty20 cricket competition, but that changed when the Kingsmen Sports Enterprise landed a successful bid.

The move also coincided with the return of the competition to Jamaica, which last hosted a CPL match when the now-defunct Tallawahs defeated Barbados Tridents in September 2019.

But amidst the buzz as the freshly branded Jamaica Kingsmen prepared to host their fourth and final home match of the 2026 season at Sabina Park late on Tuesday, Bennett noted that grassroots plans are in the pipeline.

“Certainly [hosting the games] has helped to rekindle interest in cricket. My [goal] now is to get everybody on board — both the [Kingsmen] franchise and the [Jamaican] Government — in our developmental programmes,” he told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

In February 2026 the Observer had reported that the United States-based Kingsmen group was committed to supporting grassroots development.

Kingsmen Sports Enterprise representative Faisal Mirza had said that one of the Fawad Sarwar-owned organisation’s priority is to pump resources into developing Jamaica’s young talents.

“…We definitely want to invest in grassroots and again reintegrating grassroots cricket and school cricket into the Jamaican ecosystem. Driving more of the youth into cricket… so that homegrown talent can once again sort of elevate to the levels of… the greats like Dre Russ [Andre Russell], Rovman [Powell] and Chris [Gayle] and all these legends whose shadows are often arched even beyond the game itself right,” Mirza said.

Bennett said on Tuesday that he looks forward to the investment and insisted the raw talent is available in Jamaica for players to matriculate.

“The Kingsmen are smart people. They not only want to help Jamaica’s cricket for Jamaica, they want to help Jamaica’s cricket for the Kingsmen also,” the JCA boss said.

“We have some very good youngsters around. I’m very excited about five or six Under-19 youngsters who, with the proper type of developmental programmes in place, can go very far.

“I’ve already spoken to the Kingsmen and they are very interested in our age-group programmes, and we’ve spoken to the Government who have promised to help, and also to a few sponsors who we are trying to engage,” he said.

He said he is already rubbing his hands at the prospect of implementing plans to help shape the future of Under-13 age-group players.

“We started our Under-13 programme last year and that needs to continue. We already have got invitations from both Guyana and Trinidad for our Jamaica Under-13 team to participate in tournaments there in December so we need to get busy as soon as the CPL is finished. In Jamaica — and we see other territories doing it as well — is to place the emphasis on the ground level,” Bennett said.

— Sanjay Myers

World.title: NCB resets consumer lending after delinquency spike
World.content:
NCB Financial Group Chief Executive Officer Robert Almeida says the group paused lending through recently introduced unsecured consumer products for about three months while it tightened its credit models. The affected loan book has since been relaunched and is growing with a lower delinquency rate, as NCB seeks to convert its larger deposit base into prudent new lending.

NCB Financial Group Limited (NCBFG) paused lending through recently introduced unsecured consumer products for about three months after delinquencies rose, then relaunched them with tighter credit models, Chief Executive Officer Robert Almeida said.

Almeida told the Jamaica Observer in an interview last Friday, following NCBFG’s quarterly investor briefing, that the affected loan book was growing again with a lower delinquency rate. He did not identify the products, disclose the size of the portfolio or provide delinquency rates before and after the changes.

“Consumer retail, and really unsecured consumer retail, is where we were seeing the spike in our current delinquency profile,” Almeida said.

“We took a pause for about a quarter while we tightened up those models, figured out where the weaknesses were, and then we relaunched. That loan book is now growing again, and it is growing with a lower delinquency rate.”

The intervention came during a wider contraction in NCBFG’s loan book. Gross loans and advances fell by $25.27 billion, or 3.9 per cent, to $615.57 billion at June 30 from $640.84 billion a year earlier, according to the group’s unaudited nine-month financial statements.

Almeida said the consumer-loan pause was one of several reasons for the decline. Scheduled repayments exceeded new lending during the period, while the group became more cautious following Hurricane Melissa. Management’s earlier concentration on improving basic service and attracting deposits also slowed lending, he said.

While loans declined, customer deposits rose by $67.72 billion, or 8.4 per cent, to $874.04 billion. Gross loans were equivalent to 70.4 per cent of deposits, according to a Business Observer calculation, down from 79.5 per cent a year earlier.

The movement left NCBFG with a larger pool of deposit funding relative to its loan book, but also increased the pressure on management to put that money to work without taking on excessive credit risk.

Almeida said the group was not deliberately reducing its credit exposure and wanted to reverse the decline in lending. NCB was becoming more active in motor-vehicle financing and would increase its focus on mortgages and larger corporate transactions, he said.

The delinquency spike in the newer consumer products was unrelated to the $10.67 billion in bad loans that NCBFG wrote off during the nine months to June, Almeida said. The write-offs were nearly three times the $3.75 billion recorded in the corresponding period last year.

Almeida said the write-offs covered older problem loans across the portfolio that had already been provided for.

“It included a bit of everything, because really we weren’t writing off as quickly as we should,” he said.

Removing the loans and corresponding provisions from the balance sheet therefore did not create a fresh charge against current profit. The write-offs, together with improved collections, recoveries and lower classified exposures, helped reduce non-performing loans by $4.7 billion, or 16 per cent, to $24.1 billion. The non-performing-loan ratio improved to 3.91 per cent from 4.49 per cent.

Group-wide credit impairment losses fell by 36 per cent to $4.37 billion. Almeida said current credit costs were increasingly concentrated in retail lending after several large corporate exposures produced more uneven charges in earlier periods. He said the experience with the newer consumer products had led NCBFG to tighten its underwriting.

The group’s June-quarter profit recovered from the March period, although much of the improvement came from unrealised gains on listed foreign equities rather than a comparable increase in recurring income.

Consolidated net profit rose by 57 per cent from the preceding quarter to $8.24 billion but was little changed from $8.25 billion in the corresponding period last year. Profit attributable to NCBFG shareholders increased by 30 per cent sequentially and 8.4 per cent year on year to $6.08 billion.

Gains on foreign-currency and investment activities totalled $5.74 billion, compared with a $2.01-billion loss in the March quarter — a swing of $7.75 billion.

Almeida said the foreign equities were listed and liquid, making the gains realisable, although their value remained exposed to market movements. He said averaging the March and June quarters produced what he regarded as recurring attributable profit of about $5 billion to $6 billion a quarter.

He expects that range to rise to between $6 billion and $7 billion “relatively quickly” as NCBFG works towards a return on equity of 15 to 20 per cent and a cost-to-income ratio below 60 per cent.

Those targets remain some distance away. NCBFG reported an annualised return on equity of 8.57 per cent and a nine-month cost-to-income ratio of 70.4 per cent. Its June-quarter cost-to-income ratio was approximately 66.7 per cent, based on a Business Observer calculation.

Sheree Martin, interim chief executive officer of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited, told the investor briefing that many processes at the bank remained manual, meaning efficiency improvements would be partly incremental. She said the bank was working to make its operations faster, simpler and more customer-centred, while increasing revenue to support its existing cost base.

For the nine months, net profit attributable to NCBFG shareholders fell by 30 per cent to $13.28 billion, largely because the prior-year period included a one-off gain from the sale of the group’s Netherlands insurance brokerage. NCBFG said attributable profit would have increased by 38 per cent after excluding that gain.

The group must now turn its growing deposit base into new loans while preserving the tighter credit standards introduced after the consumer-lending setback.

“The good news is, when you’re bringing in the deposits, you build up a stronger capacity to lend,” Almeida said. “Now we have to realise and utilise that capacity to grow the loan book.”

World.title: J Capri among 4 to be honoured at Excellence in Music Ceremony
World.content:
J Capri

Late dancehall star J Capri will be among four women to be honoured for their musical contributions at the Excellence in Music Ceremony 2026.

Formerly known as the Grammy Certificate Ceremony, the event will return to Jamaica in September for its 6th staging. At that time, J Capri will be posthumously awarded a British Recorded Music Industry (BPI)-certified Silver recognition for Whine & Kotch, her collaboration with Charly Black that became one of the defining songs of her career.

J Capri passed away in 2015, but Whine & Kotch continued to soar to unprecedented heights internationally.

According to organisers, the recognition will serve not only as an industry honour, but as another marker of a musical legacy that continues to outlive its creator.

Chevelle Franklyn, Heather Cummings, and Ma-Isheeba will also be recognised at the event organised by Back 2 Da Future Music Limited in partnership with Royalty Network Inc.

Franklyn is set to receive a BPI-certified Silver recognition for her contribution to Shabba Ranks’ Mr Loverman, adding to the two Grammy Certificates she received in 2024.

Heather Cummings will receive a Grammy Certificate for her contribution to Beres Hammond’s One Love, One Life, bringing her total number of recognised contributions to five, an acknowledgement of the often-unseen work of backing vocalists, whose harmonies and supporting voices can become an essential part of the character and emotional texture of a recording.

Ma-Isheeba, professionally known as Chyna, will also add another certificate to the pair she received in 2024.

Organisers say the four women to be honoured this year share a common story, one that illustrates the different ways Jamaican talent has travelled through the international music business — as featured artistes, lead voices and background singers, and through contributions to recordings that crossed genres and markets.

The latter was reiterated by Kennedy Mensah, founder of Back 2 Da Future Music Limited, who shared that greater attention needs to be given to different roles played by creatives across the industry, especially in spaces occupied by women.

“Unfortunately, music is still a heavily male-dominated business. As such, we must ensure that we take every opportunity to shine a spotlight on the ladies who have added to the very fabric of musical excellence for decades,” he said.

Mensah said this year’s cohort was deliberately selected to represent different aspects of women’s contribution to recorded music, from featured artistes such as Franklyn and J Capri, to backing vocalists Cummings and Ma-Isheeba.

The decision also reflects the changing identity of the ceremony itself. The BPI presentations were introduced on a smaller scale in 2025, when Steely and Clevie were among those recognised, and were later extended to Robert Browne at the Florida staging in January 2026. This year’s ceremony will expand the presentations in Jamaica, placing the certification honours alongside the Grammy recognitions.

More importantly, the organisers are positioning the event as an opportunity to document contributions to music that might otherwise be lost as the industry moves on to its next generation of performers and recordings.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: Jamaica edge Aruba 1-0 in CFU U14 competition
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica made it two wins in a row at the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) Under 14 Boys Tier 1 Challenge Series in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic on Tuesday, edging 10-man Aruba 1-0 to maintain their lead in Group C.

After failing to score in the first half, the first time they were held scoreless in any half over the past two tournaments, Christian Foster came off the bench to score the game’s only goal.

Jamaica are on six points, three more than St Kitts/Nevis who rebounded from their loss to Jamaica to beat Curacao 4-2 in the other Group C game.

It was a physical encounter with the referee issuing at least five yellow cards and a red to Aruba’s Sebastian Wever, a second half substitute, late in the game.

Foster scored the winner after he was left unguarded in the middle of the goal and finished off a good team movement, firing a cheeky back heel pass from Tai-Sean Headley past goalkeeper Deymar Mercado Carrillo six minutes into the second half.

Jamaica will complete their first round schedule on Wednesday when they play Curacao, starting at 12:30pm, Jamaica time.

— Paul A Reid

World.title: Hospital death probe
World.content:
An undated photo of Kenise Dunn, who died at the St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital five days after giving birth.

ADMINISTRATORS at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital say they have launched a probe into the death of Kenise Dunn, who died at the facility five days after giving birth.

With family demanding answers into the circumstances surrounding Dunn’s death, the hospital’s Chief Executive Officer Dennis Morgan told the Jamaica Observer on Monday that with internal investigations ongoing the hospital is not able to provide a statement on the matter.

According to Morgan, the investigation is integral in allowing all the facts to be found and confirmed, and for the family to be given factual answers.

Morgan added that the hospital could not legally disclose information about any patient to anyone who is not listed as their next of kin, and the administrators are already in contact with the relevant family member who has been cooperative with staff as the investigation continues.

Acknowledging the concerns held by the wider family, Morgan advised other relatives of Dunn to reach out with their questions either by calling or visiting the hospital, where they will be welcomed and briefed as best as possible.

But for Kirk Hall, uncle of the deceased, information surrounding the death of Dunn is long overdue.

Hall charged that since Dunn, who he affectionately called Punky, was admitted to hospital on July 29 up until her death on Friday, August 14, the medical staff interacting with her have not been willing to provide any information.

Tearfully recounting his niece’s last days, Hall on Monday told the Observer that Dunn, who was eight months’ pregnant, complained to him on July 27 about intense stomach pains and not being able to pass her stool for at least three days.

When told of her complications, Hall referred her to the hospital for checks to rule out anything beyond simple constipation and to ensure she received the necessary treatment.

He said when checking on his niece during her stay at the hospital he was still unable to get any information from the medical personnel as to what was causing her pain.

“When she went down there she called me and said, ‘Uncle Kirk, they might have to admit me.’ Days gone by and I asked what was going on, and she said, ‘The doctors, they keep just coming and pulling blood.’ Every day they just kept pulling blood from her while her belly continued to hurt,” said Hall.

“I said, ‘Punky I know how you feel, but it soon over.’ She called me last week, Friday [August 7] morning. So all this time, from the 29th, she has been there up ‘til when she called me…nothing had been done to her,” claimed Hall.

According to Hall, the numerous blood tests she had informed him of never provided any results, and his only update was that Dunn needed to do an ultrasound at a nearby medical facility, but no ambulance was available and the hospital was short-staffed.

“She said to me, ‘Uncle Kirk, they are supposed to carry me to go do an ultrasound. I hear the nurse just come and tell me they’re short of staff so they are not going to carry me, and the ambulance is not going to work.’ So I said, ‘Punky, what do you mean by they are short of staff and don’t have an ambulance?’ I said, ‘I’m coming to you either tomorrow or Sunday,’ ” Hall added.

He told the Observer that his Sunday visit was only more worrisome as Dunn, 33, could not tell him what was wrong with her and doctors refused to speak with him.

“When I saw her, she was on the stretcher and everything, but I can tell you, she was in pain. I said, ‘Punky, what happened?’ She said, ‘Uncle Kirk, I feel pain, man. Pain, pain, pain.’ So I said, ‘What did the doctor say?’ She said, ‘I can’t talk to them no more. You go ask them, ask them what happened to me.’

“So I went to the nurse and I asked her, ‘What’s going on with her? Can I speak to the doctor behind you?’ The nurse told me to have a seat, and about 10, 15 minutes later she came back and said the doctor says my niece can talk [for herself] and I’m not the next of kin, so she can’t talk to me,’ ” relayed Hall.

Following his visit he received a call from Dunn the next day that she was being taken to have the ultrasound done. By Tuesday it was revealed to him, by a relative who he says works at the hospital, that she had given birth.

Shortly after, he said he was told by that relative that a doctor advised him that she needed emergency surgery.

According to Hall, on that day, August 9, Dunn was placed on life support.

He said doctors briefed the family that she was gravely ill, after surgery revealed a tumour believed to be cancerous that was found in her colon. Hall charged that compounding her afflictions, the doctors said they removed the colon, and two litres of stool from her body after a bowel rupture.

Dunn never recovered, passing away five days later.

Now, the family is overcome by grief and riddled with questions. Why was the family not told about the results from the blood tests or the ultrasound? Why was she allowed to give birth naturally after being admitted for constipation? Was it ever confirmed that the tumour was malignant; was there a biopsy done? Was there even, ever a tumour?

Hall’s frustration was palpable, his voice breaking as he became overcome by emotion.

“We have requested all of that. We were told on Saturday that an investigation is going to be launched. This morning [Monday], persons from the Ministry of Health reportedly went in and seized all form of records when it come to her and the doctors, whatever they said and did to her and all of that. She didn’t deserve to die like that, man. Had there been proper care and compassion she wouldn’t die, man,” charged Hall

“We are waiting with bated breath to see what the findings are, what the results are,” Hall added.

World.title: French MEP Raphaël Glucksmann gears up to announce presidential run
World.content:
Several high-profile Socialists, including former President François Hollande and former Prime Minister Bernard Cazeneuve, have publicly hinted at plans to sit out their party’s primary and launch independent presidential bids.

However, polls show that Glucksmann, the leader of his own small political party, Place Publique, is the best-placed presidential hopeful on the center left after leading the Socialists and their allies to a strong third-place finish in the 2024 European elections.

Yet he and the rest of the field still lag significantly behind far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, according to most surveys. France’s presidential election goes to a runoff if no candidate scores more than 50 percent of the vote, and if the polls hold, Le Pen is all but guaranteed to nab one of the final two spots.

To advance to the second round, Glucksmann will have to see off centrist and center-right rivals like Edouard Philippe and the firebrand anticapitalist Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Mélenchon, who announced his plans to run in May, is currently polling slightly ahead of Glucksmann, but both are within striking distance of making the runoff.

The two are bitter rivals whose divisions are reminiscent of those across left-leaning parties in the Western world, including the U.S. Democratic Party.

World.title: UK ‘open to discussing’ digital services tax with Trump administration
World.content:
Andy Burnham speaks with staff at Wolverhampton bus station in England on Aug. 18, 2026. | Pool photo by Hannah McKay via AFP/Getty Images

Jamieson Greer said Donald Trump’s threat to slap 100% tariffs on European countries with digital services taxes is “not a bluff.”

LONDON — Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government said the U.K. is willing to discuss American concerns over its digital services tax amid renewed pressure from the White House.

President Donald Trump in June threatened to impose 100 percent tariffs on European countries with DSTs which target U.S. tech firms, and in an interview with The Times newspaper published on Monday, Trump’s top trade official Jamieson Greer said the threat was “not a bluff” and the president’s demands that foreign governments abandon such taxes were “quite serious.”

“We remain open to discussing U.S. concerns and working with partners internationally,” a U.K. government spokesperson said when asked about Greer's comments.

World.title: Reformer oder Radikaler? Ein Interview mit MV-Spitzenkandidat Leif-Erik Holm
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

In dieser Episode sprechen Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler dem Spitzenkandidaten der AfD für Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Leif-Erik Holm. Im Vorfeld der Landtagswahlen am 20. September geht es mit Holm um seine Ambitionen auf das Amt des Ministerpräsidenten und sein Vorhaben, notfalls durch eine Kooperation mit der CDU oder Tolerierungsmodelle an die Macht zu kommen. Obwohl er sich gleichzeitig die „Altparteien“ auf den „Müllhaufen der Geschichte“ wünscht.

Zudem konfrontieren die beiden Holm mit seiner energiepolitischen Kernforderung nach einer Rückkehr zu russischem Gas. Sie haken nach, wie sich diese Strategie mit den Importverboten der EU und dem Angriffskrieg Russlands gegen die Ukraine vereinbaren lässt und ob die AfD damit nicht sehenden Auges neue energie- und sicherheitspolitische Abhängigkeiten für Deutschland in Kauf nimmt.

Ein weiterer kritischer Fokus des Interviews liegt auf dem Personal des Landesverbandes.

Schindler und von Pezold befragen Holm zum neuen Generalsekretär seiner Partei sowie Vorstandsmitgliedern der Parteijugend Generation Deutschland, die teils eine Vergangenheit in der rechtsextremen NPD haben.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
